text: Lesson 27 built a pull that assumes Meridian HR always answers instantly with a clean 200. Production doesn't work that way. This lesson adds what Chapter 6 taught — retries, idempotency, and checkpoint logging — to make this integration survive the failures that will actually happen.

Three real gaps show up the moment this runs in production: a transient network blip during the pull, Meridian HR returning a 500 while it deploys its own changes, and the real possibility that Meridian redelivers the same webhook notification twice. None of these are hypothetical — they are exactly the failure modes Chapter 6's error-handling lessons warned about, now showing up inside a real, working integration.

The retry loop only retries on a 5xx status or a thrown exception — a transient problem on Meridian HR's side. A 400 or 404 means the request itself is wrong, and retrying it just repeats the same failure three times instead of once. Each retry waits longer than the last — exponential backoff — instead of hammering a struggling system.

Before creating a sys_user, the script queries for one that already has this employee's Meridian ID. If Meridian HR redelivers the same webhook, this check is what stops a second, duplicate sys_user from ever getting created — the idempotency property Chapter 6 built toward.

An orchestrator method ties it together: pull with retries, bail out and log an error if every attempt failed, otherwise create the pending user and the onboarding task set. Nothing downstream ever runs on a partial or missing employee record.

Every checkpoint in this flow gets a log line of its own: gs.info fires when the pull succeeds, when a retry is about to happen, and when an existing user gets skipped — none of those three are failures, just normal operation worth a record. gs.error is reserved for retries fully exhausted and genuinely malformed responses — exactly the cases a real on-call engineer needs to see without digging.

Authentication, the pull, retries, idempotency, and logging are all real now. Lesson 29 closes this capstone with the test plan a working developer would actually write before calling this integration done.
